questions.q: State the formal definition of Big-O notation: f(n) = O(g(n)) if and only if there exist positive constants c and n₀ such that... (complete the definition).
questions.a: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff ∃ c > 0, n₀ > 0 such that 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. A wrong answer (e.g., "f(n) ≤ g(n) for all n" or missing constants) reveals the student treats Big-O as exact equality or ignores the "eventually" nature of asymptotic bounds — they confuse tight bounds with loose upper bounds and cannot prove membership formally.

questions.q: Explain why the statement "Algorithm A with time complexity 100n + 5 is faster than Algorithm B with time complexity 0.01n² for all input sizes" is false, and determine the crossover point where B becomes slower than A.
questions.a: For small n (n < 10,000), 100n + 5 < 0.01n², so A is actually faster initially. The crossover occurs at n ≈ 10,000 where 100n = 0.01n² → n = 10,000. A wrong answer (claiming A is always faster or always slower) reveals the student ignores constant factors and lower-order terms entirely, misunderstanding that asymptotic dominance only applies for sufficiently large n — a critical error when choosing algorithms for real-world constrained inputs.

questions.q:
Analyse the time complexity of the following pseudocode fragment in terms of n. Show your counting of basic operations.
```
for i = 1 to n do
    for j = 1 to i do
        x = x + 1
    end for
end for
```
questions.a: The inner loop runs i times for each i from 1 to n. Total executions = Σ(i=1 to n) i = n(n+1)/2 = ½n² + ½n. Basic operation (assignment) executes Θ(n²) times. A wrong answer of O(n) or O(n³) reveals the student either treats the inner loop as constant-time or misapplies multiplication rule for nested loops — they fail to recognise the variable upper bound j ≤ i creates a triangular summation, not a rectangular n×n grid.

questions.q:
Compare the space complexity of these two recursive algorithms for factorial(n):
Algorithm R1: if n=0 return 1 else return n * R1(n-1)
Algorithm R2: iterative version using a single accumulator variable.
Which uses more space asymptotically and why?
questions.a: R1 uses Θ(n) space due to n recursive calls on the call stack (each storing return address, parameters, local variables). R2 uses Θ(1) auxiliary space (only accumulator and loop counter). R1 uses more space asymptotically. A wrong answer claiming both are O(1) reveals the student ignores call stack overhead in recursion — a classic senior-secondary error where space complexity is conflated with variable count only, missing the implicit memory cost of function call frames.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "Since merge sort has Θ(n log n) worst-case time and bubble sort has Θ(n²), merge sort is always the better choice for sorting." Provide two concrete scenarios where bubble sort could be preferred despite worse asymptotic complexity.
questions.a: The claim is false. Bubble sort may be preferred when: (1) n is very small (e.g., n ≤ 50) where constant factors dominate and bubble sort's simplicity avoids recursion overhead; (2) the array is already nearly sorted — bubble sort with early termination runs in O(n) best case while merge sort still does Θ(n log n). A wrong answer (agreeing with the claim or giving irrelevant scenarios) reveals the student treats asymptotic complexity as the sole decision criterion, ignoring constant factors, best-case behaviour, stability, in-place requirement, and implementation simplicity — all practical considerations in board exam case-study questions.

questions.q: Design a pseudocode algorithm that finds the maximum element in an unsorted array of size n with Θ(n) time and Θ(1) auxiliary space. Then modify it to also return the index of the maximum element without increasing asymptotic complexity. Explain why your modification preserves Θ(1) space.
questions.a:
```
max = A[0]; idx = 0
for i = 1 to n-1 do
    if A[i] > max then
        max = A[i]; idx = i
    end if
end for
return (max, idx)
```
Time: n-1 comparisons → Θ(n). Auxiliary space: only max, idx, i → Θ(1). Modification adds one integer variable (idx), which is O(1) — constants don't affect asymptotic space. A poor answer (using extra array, recursion, or claiming space becomes O(n)) reveals the student confuses output size with auxiliary space, or thinks any additional variable changes asymptotic class — misunderstanding that Θ(1) means "bounded by a constant independent of n".
